crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Explaining research after publication covers the work of turning a finished paper into clear summaries, annotations, and discussions for readers beyond the original authors. It includes plain-language abstracts, visual abstracts, author question and answer sessions, journal clubs, and post-publication peer review. The goal is to make methods, findings, and limits understandable without simplifying away uncertainty. This work sits between the published record and the wider research community, including clinicians, policymakers, and students.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the published paper itself, its supplementary materials, and any registered data or code. It also draws on preprint servers, publisher platforms, and indexing systems that carry version-of-record metadata. For AI-assisted explanation, the infrastructure includes text extraction, citation parsing, and retrieval over a paper library, but the source of truth remains the original article. No explanation should rely on a secondary search tool when the primary paper is available.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The typical method starts with close reading of the abstract, methods, results, and limitations, then restates the research question, design, and main findings in plain language. Writers check each claim against the paper's own evidence and flag where the authors themselves express uncertainty. When AI is used, it can help extract claims, suggest simpler phrasing, or map jargon to glossary terms, but a human reviewer verifies every output against the original text. The result is a layered explanation: a short summary for skimming, a longer walkthrough for careful readers, and notes on what the study does not show.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on accuracy, attribution, and the boundary between explanation and endorsement. An explanation must not alter the authors' meaning, overstate effect sizes, or imply clinical or policy advice the paper does not support. It should link to the original paper and respect copyright by summarising rather than reproducing large passages. Provenance matters: readers need to know whether a summary was written by the authors, an independent expert, or an AI system, and whether it has been checked. Post-publication commentary can also carry reputational risk, so corrections and version notes should be visible.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The practice is moving toward structured, machine-readable explanations that travel with a paper across platforms. Publishers and funders are encouraging plain-language summaries and registered post-publication review, while AI tools are becoming better at drafting explanations from full text and flagging unsupported claims. The likely direction is a linked ecosystem where a paper carries its own explainer, its critical appraisals, and its provenance trail, all updated as new evidence appears. The hard part will remain judging what a study actually supports, not just restating it.
